rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology and Results sections <U+2013> the authors develop the WEBSOM algorithm (k-means sector identification plus a customized NSGA-II) and run it on the Palos de la Frontera irrigation district network (227 hydrants, 3 pumping stations), reporting their own optimization outputs (Tables 1-3, Figs 5-6).
rows.notes: The study does describe exactly what the passage says: sectors are defined by dimensionless topological coordinates and k-means, then NSGA-II produces a monthly sectoring/pumping calendar minimizing F1 (energy consumption + irrigation deficit) and F2 (hydrants below service pressure + magnitude of pressure deficit). However, the reliability outcome (irrigation deficit eliminated from generation 2, only 1-7 hydrants below 30 m, 20-29% energy savings) is obtained purely from EPANET hydraulic simulation driven by design flows (qmax x hydrant area, all hydrants in a sector open) and theoretical irrigation requirements; no model output is compared with telemetry pressures or flows from the real network. The only comparison with measured data is the current energy consumption (4115 MWh, from Rodr<U+00ED>guez D<U+00ED>az et al. 2011), which is a baseline for the savings estimate rather than a validation of the simulated pressures or deficits. Under the rule that a model run on design data or never checked against observations does not count, Q2 is answered no. Had Q2 been yes: single district (Q5 no), scheme scale (Q6 would be yes), authors note pressure deficits would be tolerable for drip and that full demand with all hydrants open rarely occurs concurrently (a qualification rather than a stated limitation), results reported as ranges across Pareto solutions but no dispersion/uncertainty analysis.

notes: Full text appears complete (post-print with tables and figures). The study is a simulation/optimization case study on one Spanish irrigation district; the hydraulic model is not validated against observed data within the paper.
